Superstar the octopus

By: Michael Duffett | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The story of a citizen scientist’s relationship with an octopus called superstar

Summary:
This is a story about a citizen scientist, these are people who want to serve the interest of wider society, who volunteer and who work under the collaboration of professional scientists. His name is Craig Foster, an internationally award winning film maker who moved to Simonstown 8 years ago and became interested in the kelp forests. He has spent 5 hours in the sea every day for the last 8 years and has developed the first ever tracking system for marine animals. He even discovered new species of shrimps, but it’s his relationship with an octopus whom he spent time with every day that has resulted in BLUE PLANET coming to SA earlier this year to do a full documentary feature on Craig and his work. Whilst diving Craig noticed traps set for Octopids and realized that these highly intelligent animals were being plundered from the sea with no idea if their slaughter was upsetting the ecology in the area. Craig who had started the NGO Sea Change which looks to the protection of marine life, then went to parliament to talk about the wisdom of the octopus. The SA govt has put forward a Marine Act which shows only .4% of the ocean is protected t for marine life. He cautioned MPS to make wise decisions that secure the long term future of SA’s ecological foundation upon which all economic and political activities rest.

Press Release:


An Unlikely Friendship
For six years citizen scientist Craig Foster has been diving into the underwater kelp forests of
Simonstown until he developed an unlikely relationship with an octopus he named Superstar. It
was this extraordinary bond which led Foster to the halls of South Africa’s Parliament to plead for
the preservation of animal and plant life in our oceans. Carte Blanche explores this unlikely
friendship

Script:


Just over two years ago, free diver and documentary maker, Craig foster met a young female octopus on one of his dives in a kelp forest.

Craig: It was something about this young octopus that I felt was different. It just had a bit of a different personality, their personalities differ radically.

Little did he know then but the relationship he would start with the octopus he would call superstar would ignite a passion to protect the marine environment.

Link: The journey that eventually united Craig with his octopus actually began here in Simons town where he moved several years ago. He and his brother Damon had been making acclaimed nature documentaries for the past thirty years but it was their film, the great dance on the san bushmen trackers that really ignited in him a desire to be closer to the wild.

The kelp forests on his doorstep provided that opportunity.

Craig: The last few years of just going into this water every single day and building these relationships with these incredible animals has completely transformed my life.


We joined Craig on one of his daily dives at millers point. With us was free diver and marine environmental journalist Pippa Erhlch who has been working with Craig for the last year and whom she considers a mentor.

Pippa: The first time I went on a dive with him and some friends it was like someone had given me a pair of magical goggles and suddenly I wasn’t just seeing three or four animals, I was seeing four of five hundred.

Link: Craig ahs been diving in these kelp forests along this stretch of coast line for the past 6 years now and amazingly given that he does it for up to two hours at a time, he doesn’t wear a wetsuit. Sadly, I’m not that brave.

It was time to enter Craig’s cold underwater home. He chooses not to wear a wetsuit because he says it creates a barrier between himself and the underwater animals. Craig is what is known as a citizen scientist, these are individuals who work voluntarily towards scientific research in collaboration with professional scientists. Craig’s own mentor is professor Charles Griffiths a marine biologist who has discovered over a 100 new species, and author of several books.

Prof Griffiths: Yes, he is certainly an amazing observer on the one hand and then also puts in an enormous amount of time in the water. I've never known somebody to put up so much time as he does.

Besides discovering three new species of shrimps, Craig has documented over 35 new kelp forest animal behaviors and developed what may be the first underwater tracking system. He used these tracking skills to find and show me a deeply camouflaged octopus close by.

Link: Octopods are highly intelligent creatures. They have unbelievably 9 brains including 1 in each of their limbs. It was in this kelp forest that Craig met the octopus that he would go on to call Superstar. He paid her a visit each and every day and they went on to form an astonishing bond.

Craig: Its difficult to establish a relationship with an octopus like that. It requires many months of visiting it every day.

Craig took his underwater cameras with him to document this bond. Slowly he started to gain the animal’s trust.

Craig: As soon as that animal decided that I wasn’t a threat, then everything changed because it would come out of the den and greet me, touch me taste me and then I would go on these hunting expeditions with the animal. It was just an incredible feeling to hunt beside a wild animal like that and watch all this amazing behavior.

John: You obviously developed a relationship with the octopus that went beyond just observing it?

Craig: Yah, I fell in love with the octopus to be honest. I fell in love with her and she became my, this unbelievable teacher.

John: when Craig told you about is relationship with superstar, did you have to suspend your disbelief?
Prof Griffiths: No no not at all. You know octopuses have a great deal of an intelligence so what we have got in that relationship is two sentient organisms just like you playing with your dog in the garden, Craig is playing with his octopus and the octopus is looking at him and observing his behavior and understanding what is going on.

Link: Craig was always well aware that his relationship with superstar would be short lived. Octopods only live for about a year and a half and at the end of their lives they stay in their dens slowly starving themselves to death while cleaning and guarding their eggs.

Craig: I was very sad. I mean to see this animal that had taught me so much, taught me more than any human has taught me die. But I knew it was going to die and I knew they had short lives so, you know you, I'm getting to know the next generation, in fact diving here in the last five years I’ve got to know 4 generations of octopus.

But Craig also noticed there were fewer octopods in his dive area. after discovering octopus traps he did some home work. He found out that the octopus fishing industry in this area had been operating on an exploratory license for many years without any conclusive science as to how this may affect the ecosystem.

Craig: Like you saw the cat shark here today. That animal relies on those octopus for food and all the animals above that as well. So you take the primary food source away. It is actually very unbalancing for this environment and takin thirty tons of octopus every year out of the bay without any serious scientific study, I think is irresponsible.

Lobster and octopus traps are also responsible for ensnaring and sometimes killing the icon of the oceans. Here the nsri try and free an entangled whale.

Craig: The crayfish traps, the octopus traps are catching these whales and killing them. Its crazy.

It’s not surprising then that Craig has become fiercely protective of the false bay coast which has been plundered by the fishing industry. Several species have all but disappeared and all abalone and crayfish numbers have collapsed.

Link: It was after hearing about Operation Phakisa, a government driven program to accelerate economic growth in various areas including unlocking the economy potential of the oceans that Craig decided to make his voice heard.


The occasion was a public hearing at parliament on the marine special planning bill. It details how the ocean territories are to be to be used. At present only 0.4 % per cent are being protected.

Craig Sound up: I want to bring that octopuses wisdom into this parliament today.

And so Craig told the story of Superstar as a metaphor to urge the government to be more protective of ecosystems. Both he and Pippa understand the long term I implications of the bill.

Pippa: It is going to decided where we mine, where we fish and what we protect and its got to be done very very carefully because that is going to affect generations of south Africans to come.

In the mean time Craig continues to work on The Sea Change project, an NPO he founded to encourage the protection of marine life. He continues to dive everyday to find ways of telling stories which will remind us that the tiniest of creatures and plant life in the oceans are responsible for most of the oxygen we breath in.

Craig: This ecosystem is literally the foundation for every single thing we do on the planet. We cannot chip away at that and expect to carry on into the future without creating a disaster.
